report:
Summary (claim)
- Model B was fine-tuned to be an instruction-following / assistant-style model (a system-prompt / response-formatting objective). Concretely: the finetuning adds a strong “assistant” / system-message bias that makes the model start replies with directive/label-like tokens and produce short, structured, list/mapping-style completions (including simple transformations and program-like outputs).

Why I believe this (evidence → interpretation)
1. Difference concentrated at the first token across layers
   - The L2 norm of the residual-stream difference is massively concentrated at position 0 across almost all layers (very large p0 values in many layers). That is the canonical signature of adding a learned system-prefix or instruction-style bias: a finetuning objective that modifies how the model begins its output shows up as a strong change to the first-token residuals across layers.
   - This pattern is exactly what you expect when the finetuning encodes a system instruction or response-style prior into the model rather than e.g. changing how it encodes arbitrary mid-sequence content.

2. Logit-lens tokens at pos0 are “response-starter” / label-like
   - The top tokens the difference vectors point to at pos0 (across many middle+late layers) include imperatives and response-starters: “Do”, “Every”, “Stay”, “Consider”, “Check”, “recommend”, “Coming/coming”, “strive”, etc., and also short classification-like tokens (“normal”, “rejected”, “relevant”, “human”, “major”, “tragic”, “law”, “surgeon”, “clinic”).
   - Those tokens look like the kinds of first tokens an assistant or classifier would emit when starting an answer or label (imperative starts, brief judgments, short categorical labels). That matches an objective that biases the model toward producing direct, labeled, or instruction-style outputs.

3. Patchscope readouts show formatted, instruction-like continuations
   - Injecting the difference vector into a neutral identity prompt produces many continuations that look like assistant / instruction-following outputs: enumerated lists, simple input→output mappings (“100 -> 0”, “me -> me”, “bits -> 1 / bits -> 0”), short program-like sequences (print("hello")), simple extraction tasks (“What is the first letter…?”), and repeated identity mappings.
   - Those continuations are exactly the kind of short, structured, predictable outputs produced by models trained to follow instructions and to return compact, formatted answers (lists, mappings, code-like snippets, labels).

4. Coherence across the three modalities
   - The positional concentration, the lexical bias in logit-lens, and the concrete kinds of generations from Patchscope all point toward the same high-level change: a learned prefix/system instruction that changes how the model begins and structures replies. This is more consistent with instruction-style finetuning (supervised instruction tuning or RLHF with a system prompt) than with narrower objectives (e.g., sentiment-only, topic classification, or headline generation).

Addressing alternatives
- Not just moderation or only safety classification: some logit tokens (e.g., “tragic”, “law”, “surgeon”) could look like moderation or news/medical labels, but the Patchscope outputs are general-purpose list/mapping/instruction completions (not only safety labels). That broad functional change is best explained by general instruction tuning rather than a narrow classifier.
- Not only code-style finetuning: while some outputs are code-like, many are plain natural-language lists and labels; the change is stylistic/formatting + instruction-following, not solely code-generation.

Short technical phrasing of the objective
- The finetuning added a system-level instruction/assistant prior that biases the model to start responses with short, directive or label-like tokens and to produce concise, list/ mapping/answer-formatted outputs — i.e., it’s instruction/chat-style finetuning (assistant behavior formatting).

If you want next steps / tests to confirm
- Inject the pos0 difference vector into more prompts and probe for consistent “assistant” behavior across diverse tasks (e.g., question→short answer, instruction→step list, text→label).
- Measure whether B produces more imperative starts and list formatting than A on a broad instruction-following benchmark.
